prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the precision CMB candidate (B055) to the optical lattice clock (B030) with Katori and Ye as a single part. The scientific reasons are these. The magic-wavelength idea is a new physical mechanism and not a refinement: it cancels the lattice light shift, removes Doppler and recoil effects, and lets thousands of atoms be interrogated together. It has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and China, with clock comparisons agreeing near 10^-18, so the maturity is real. Its reach into fundamental physics is already demonstrated at the level that matters to me as a theorist who wants clues from nature: relativistic redshift resolved across millimetres and tighter limits on drifting constants, with dark-matter searches as a prospect rather than a result. Most decisive for the final stage, the credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the scheme, Ye drove it to the accuracy and many-body regime, and every member who proposed laureates named exactly these two. I would word the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realization, and leave applications and the pending redefinition of the second out of it. I still believe the CMB measurement is the discovery that speaks most directly to the structure of the universe, but a prize cannot rest on my conviction alone when the name set is unresolved.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B030 is that it is a precision-measurement invention sitting next to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, and whether that counts as discovery or invention in the statutory sense is a fair question. My answer is that the idea of trapping at a magic wavelength is distinct from both, but I accept that the committee must decide this consciously and not by head count. The societal and fundamental payoff is partly prospective until the second is redefined. Priority outside the credited names (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Hollberg) has not been settled by expert report and could change how credit is described. For my former candidate, B055 remains mature and scientifically central but suffers from the WMAP versus Planck allocation and from the earlier COBE prize; I have not seen a trio that the committee could defend on both satellites.

responses.point: Pearce argues that no fair trio exists for B055 because Page and Bennett built and calibrated WMAP, Spergel did the parameter analysis and Puget leads Planck HFI, so any three exclude a satellite team or an instrument builder, and he asks whether Bennett, Spergel and Puget can be defended on the Planck side.
responses.response: Having thought about it since round 1, I cannot defend it to the standard I would demand of someone else's candidate. A trio of Bennett, Spergel and Puget represents the analysis and one Planck instrument, while your Bennett, Spergel and Page trio is a WMAP-only prize. Each leaves out a part of how percent-level precision was reached. I see no principled way to choose between them without an expert report, and the committee does not have one. That is why I now put B030 first, with two agreed names. I keep B055 as an alternative because the science is not in doubt, but I will not press an unresolved name set against a settled one.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B030 first and says she would cite the magic-wavelength lattice trapping and its realization in clocks together, because the idea is what is new and the clock is what shows it works, and she also asks the committee to hear why Pearce and Olsson were less convinced that the discovery content is more than metrological.
responses.response: I agree with the citation framing and have used it. A citation for the clock alone would blur the line to 2005 and 2012, whereas the magic-wavelength trap states what is new. I also take the point that agreement between atomic physicists should not be over-trusted. As a non-atomic physicist I find the new-mechanism argument convincing, and I am persuaded by the independent reproduction across several continents more than by the prospective applications. Where I would press you is on the share question: the committee should say plainly that Katori's concept and first demonstration and Ye's route to 10^-18 are both decisive, and an expert report should check Lemonde's early work before the final ballot.

responses.point: Olsson says that COBE already received the original CMB anisotropy discovery, that WMAP and Planck are a later and more precise version of the same measurement, and that she would need a convincing argument that a precision refinement is a new discovery. She has now moved to B030 as her first choice.
responses.response: I still think she undervalues what changed between COBE and WMAP. The acoustic peaks and a flat universe with a percent-level matter and dark-energy budget were not in COBE. But I concede that this is a debatable line, and her test of whether the credited people actually did the original work is exactly the one B055 fails to pass cleanly. On B030 her point that the two original steps are Katori's proposal and demonstration and Ye's accuracy and many-body work persuades me. I also agree with her that applications should stay out of the citation. I have no tie to Tokyo or JILA, so her fellowship does not affect my reading of the case.

responses.point: Kroll sees IceCube's source identification as thin and the discovery as perhaps slightly early, while he regards the lattice clock as an instrument that changed what can be measured, as the chair summary also records.
responses.response: I only partly agree. The diffuse astrophysical flux is established in several channels and I would not call the discovery premature, and that is why I keep B020 as a second alternative. But his caution about source identification is a reasonable argument for waiting, and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND credit needs an expert report before any three names are defended. A second prize part from B020 alongside B030 would exceed the three-person limit. On the timing of the clock he is right that the planned redefinition of the second makes recognition current, though I treat that as a supporting argument and not a basis for the credit.

uncertainties: Whether an expert report would find a priority claim (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Hollberg) that changes the two-name credit or the wording of the shares between Katori and Ye.

Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement invention as discovery or invention in the statutory sense given the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I believe the magic-wavelength mechanism separates it, but this is a judgment the committee should make explicitly.

Whether B055 could return as a well-defined WMAP-and-Planck prize once the committee agrees a rule for large satellite collaborations; I am less sure of this than I was in round 1 and the Hubble tension may also affect the framing.
Whether any second part (for example B020) is both distinct and fairly credited within three persons; with Katori and Ye already two names I do not see one.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have a professional interest in dark-energy cosmology but no institutional, collaborative or personal tie to Katori, Ye, Bennett, Spergel, Puget, Page or any other shortlisted person. Olsson's Tokyo fellowship and Kroll's JILA lineage were disclosed in round 1; I do not consider either a bar to voting, but I would be content to follow the committee's rule on discounting.
